query: Single-phase high-entropy alloys have difficulty achieving a satisfactory strength–ductility balance. Earlier work introduced the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy with a uniform, fine lamellar structure to enable large-sized production and obtain good strength and plasticity, but its performance still falls short of industrial requirements. Its use in aircraft and spacecraft fasteners further requires stability under extreme temperature fluctuations, long-term mechanical loading, room-temperature creep, and corrosion, while relevant creep and corrosion studies remain limited by sample-size and experimental-environment constraints. Given these limitations and design requirements, what single intervention could improve the alloy’s practical performance? Present one hypothesis that specifies the intervention, causal mechanism, predicted improvement over the starting material, boundary conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a feasible experiment whose outcome could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A single thermomechanical treatment—specifically, cryogenic rolling followed by a brief, controlled annealing step—will refine the eutectic lamellar microstructure into a hierarchical architecture that simultaneously boosts yield and ultimate tensile strengths without a major loss in ductility.
generation.material_initial_state: AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy in the as‐cast condition exhibiting a fine lamellar fcc/B2 dual-phase structure with known high strength (~944–1186 MPa fracture stress) and moderate ductility (~22–26% elongation) at room temperature.
generation.intervention: Apply cryogenic deformation (e.g., 8% reduction by cryo-rolling) followed by short-duration annealing (e.g., around 700 °C for a few minutes) to partially recrystallize and refine the lamellar microstructure.
generation.conditions: The process should be performed under controlled cryogenic conditions and annealed at a temperature sufficiently high to trigger partial recrystallization yet low enough to preserve the dual-phase lamellar morphology; mechanical testing should then be conducted at ambient and elevated temperatures to assess stability.
generation.structural_mediator: A hierarchical microstructure characterized by ultrafine grains within the retained lamellae and enhanced phase boundaries that are both strong and ductile.
generation.mechanism: Cryogenic rolling generates a high dislocation density and heterogeneous strain across the distinct phases. Subsequent controlled annealing promotes partial recrystallization and grain refinement without complete loss of the lamellar architecture. This refined microstructure increases dislocation barrier density (through grain boundaries and refined lamellar spacing) thereby raising yield and ultimate strengths while maintaining sufficient work hardening for ductility. In addition, the preserved lamellar interfaces help stabilize the material’s performance under high-temperature fluctuations and corrosive environments.
generation.predicted_outcome: The treated alloy is expected to exhibit a noticeable increase in yield and ultimate tensile strengths (potentially in the range of several hundred MPa improvement over the as-cast state) while preserving or only slightly reducing ductility, making it more suitable for the rigors of aerospace fastener applications.
generation.baseline: The as-cast AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy with a fracture stress near 1.2 GPa (true stress condition) and ductility around 22–26% at room temperature.
generation.boundary: The improvement is contingent on maintaining a balance between refinement and retention of the dual-phase lamellar structure. Excessive deformation or annealing that completely eliminates the lamellar morphology may lead to unacceptably low ductility or degradation in high-temperature and corrosion performance.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative gains in strength and ductility, and the long-term stability of the refined structure under service conditions, remain uncertain until validated by systematic mechanical and microstructural studies.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a set of AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy samples. Process one group by standard casting (baseline) and a second group by applying cryogenic rolling (e.g., 8% reduction) followed by annealing at 700 °C for a short duration (e.g., 2–15 minutes). Conduct tensile tests at room and elevated temperatures, microstructural characterization (using TEM/SEM) to quantify grain and lamellar refinement, and creep/corrosion tests under conditions matching aerospace service environments.
measurements: Tensile stress–strain curves to determine yield strength, ultimate tensile strength and elongation
Electron microscopy (SEM/TEM) to measure grain size, lamellar spacing and phase distribution
Corrosion resistance assessments in relevant simulated environments
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the cryo-rolled and annealed samples do not demonstrate statistically significant improvements in both strength and ductility (or if the microstructural refinement compromises high-temperature stability or corrosion resistance compared to the as-cast alloy), then the hypothesis—that this treatment intervention can overcome the strength–ductility tradeoff—is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Thermodynamics calculations based on the CALPHAD (calculation of phase diagrams) method can also provide an insightful guidance to design EHEAs, on the premise that reliable thermodynamics database for HEAs are to be established and completed. In summary, here we proposed a novel strategy to design high-entropy alloys (HEAs), i.e., the concept of eutectic high-entropy alloys (EHEAs), to solve the challenging issues for this new type of advanced metallic materials, including the conflict between high fracture strength and high ductility, and the inferior castability and compositional segregation. Based on the new strategy, we successfully designed a highly uniform AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA, with an unprecedented combination of castability, high fracture strength and high ductility. The bulk EHEA ingot of ~2.5 kg in weight was prepared by the conventional casting method using the commercially pure raw materials. The EHEA exhibited a fine lamellar microstructure consisting of coupled grown fcc/B2 phases. Our design strategy is of great significance in both scientific and technical aspects, and can be readily adapted to large-scale industrial production of HEAs.

Nano-lamellar (L12 + B2) AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high entropy alloy (EHEA) was processed by cryo-rolling and annealing. The EHEA developed a novel hierarchical microstructure featured by fine lamellar regions consisting of FCC lamellae filled with ultrafine FCC grains (average size ~200–250 nm) and B2 lamellae, and coarse non-lamellar regions consisting of ultrafine FCC (average size ~200–250 nm), few coarse recrystallized FCC grains and rather coarse unrecrystallized B2 phase (~2.5 µm). This complex and hierarchical microstructure originated from differences in strain-partitioning amongst the constituent phases, affecting the driving force for recrystallization. The hierarchical microstructure of the cryo-rolled and annealed material resulted in simultaneous enhancement in strength (Yield Strength/YS: 1437 ± 26 MPa, Ultimate Tensile Strength/UTS: 1562 ± 33 MPa) and ductility (elongation to failure/ef ~ 14 ± 1%) as compared to the as-cast as well as cold-rolled and annealed materials.
